lessonTitle: Special Stains, Immunohistochemistry and Electron Microscopy

blocks.text: A lung biopsy from an immunosuppressed patient looks like patchy inflammation on routine haematoxylin and eosin. The diagnosis hinges on whether special stains reveal fungal walls, iron pigment or acid-fast organisms, and whether antibody stains identify the cells involved. H&E answers general questions; other methods answer specific ones.

blocks.markdown: Each method reveals a different level of detail. A **special (histochemical) stain** uses a chemical reaction or dye affinity to show a class of tissue component. **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)** uses an antibody to locate one specific protein antigen. **Electron microscopy** uses electrons instead of light for far higher resolution.

blocks.title: PAS and immunohistochemistry
blocks.text: The periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain demonstrates carbohydrate-rich structures: periodic acid oxidises vicinal diols in sugars to aldehydes, which react with Schiff reagent to give a magenta colour. It stains glycogen, neutral mucins, basement membranes, brush borders and fungal cell walls. Treating a section with the enzyme diastase first digests glycogen, so PAS staining that disappears after diastase is glycogen. IHC applies a specific primary antibody to the section, then an enzyme-labelled secondary antibody; an enzyme such as horseradish peroxidase converts a chromogen (commonly DAB) to a brown deposit where the antigen is located.

blocks.markdown: IHC is used to identify tissue of origin (for example cytokeratins for epithelial cells, CD markers for lymphocyte types), to detect markers that guide treatment (for example HER2 or hormone receptors in breast cancer), and to estimate proliferation with **Ki-67**, a protein expressed in cycling cells. The **Ki-67 labelling index** is the percentage of tumour nuclei that stain: $\text{index} = \text{positive nuclei}/\text{total nuclei counted} \times 100\%$. Good IHC needs controls and, after formalin fixation, often **antigen retrieval**.

blocks.title: Choosing a stain
blocks.prompt: A liver biopsy is suspected to show iron overload. Which stain, and what result?

steps.text: Iron deposits (haemosiderin) are not highlighted well by H&E.
Perls Prussian blue reacts with ferric iron to give a blue pigment.
Blue granules in hepatocytes would confirm iron deposition.

blocks.markdown: **Light versus electron microscopy.** The resolution limit of a light microscope is about $d = 0.61\lambda/\text{NA}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength and NA the numerical aperture of the objective. With visible light (about 400-700 nm) and high NA this gives about 200 nm. In **transmission electron microscopy (TEM)**, a beam of electrons passes through an ultrathin section (about 60-90 nm), after fixation in glutaraldehyde, osmium tetroxide post-fixation and contrast from heavy metals such as uranyl acetate and lead citrate. The theoretical resolution is about 0.2 nm, but for biological sections about 1-2 nm is realistic. TEM images are monochrome (grey), require a vacuum, and show a tiny field, but resolve ribosomes, membranes, junctions, mitochondrial cristae and basement membrane detail invisible by light microscopy. **Scanning electron microscopy** images surfaces rather than internal structure.

blocks.title: Calculating light microscope resolution
blocks.prompt: Using green light of wavelength 550 nm with an objective of NA 1.30, what is the smallest resolvable distance?

steps.text: d = 0.61 x 550 / 1.30 = 258 nm, so structures closer than about 0.26 micrometres blur together.

items: Use special stains to show classes of molecules and organisms; use IHC to show one specific antigen.
PAS: glycogen, mucin, basement membrane, fungi; diastase distinguishes glycogen.
TEM gives ultrastructure at 1-2 nm in practice but needs ultrathin sections and heavy metal contrast.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A special stain is a chemical reaction that highlights a class of molecule; IHC is an antibody binding reaction aimed at one antigen. Do not quote 0.2 nm as typical TEM resolution for tissue sections.

points: PAS demonstrates carbohydrate-rich material (glycogen, mucin, basement membrane, fungi), and IHC uses antibodies to localise specific antigens such as cytokeratin or Ki-67.
Matching a stain to a target (trichrome, Perls, Congo red, Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen, silver) is a core diagnostic skill.
Light microscopy resolves about 200 nm, whereas TEM resolves about 1-2 nm in tissue and shows ultrastructure.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from an infant shows hepatocytes full of magenta granules after PAS staining. After pre-treatment with diastase, the magenta staining disappears. What was the material?

distractorRationale.b: Mucin is not digested by diastase.
distractorRationale.c: Basement membrane staining persists after diastase.
distractorRationale.d: Iron is not demonstrated by PAS.

questions.explanation: PAS stains carbohydrate-rich material, and diastase digests glycogen specifically. Staining that is PAS-positive before and negative after diastase is therefore glycogen.

questions.stem: A poorly differentiated metastasis in a lymph node must be shown to be epithelial rather than lymphoid in origin. Which method is most suitable?
questions.explanation: IHC uses an antibody to detect a specific protein; cytokeratins are intermediate filament proteins of epithelial cells. A positive result supports epithelial origin.

questions.stem: A patient with hereditary iron overload has a liver biopsy. Which stain demonstrates haemosiderin?

distractorRationale.d: Elastic van Gieson shows elastic fibres.

questions.explanation: Perls reagent reacts with ferric iron in haemosiderin to form blue pigment. The other stains are directed at different components.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy from a patient with long-standing myeloma shows amorphous pink deposits. Which stain and observation would support amyloid?

options.text: Congo red, with apple-green birefringence under polarised light
Perls Prussian blue, with blue granules

questions.correctOptionText: Congo red, with apple-green birefringence under polarised light

distractorRationale.d: Trichrome shows collagen in blue or green.

questions.explanation: Congo red binds amyloid fibrils, which then show apple-green birefringence under polarised light. This is a classic special-stain confirmation.

questions.stem: A sputum smear from a patient with a chronic cough and weight loss is examined for tuberculosis. Which stain is appropriate and what is expected?

options.text: Gram stain, with all bacteria purple
Congo red, with green birefringent bacteria

distractorRationale.b: Mycobacteria stain poorly with Gram stain because of their waxy wall.
distractorRationale.c: PAS stains fungal walls and carbohydrates.

questions.explanation: Mycobacteria have a lipid-rich wall that resists decolourisation by acid-alcohol after carbol fuchsin, so they appear red with Ziehl-Neelsen. Gram stain is unreliable for them.

questions.stem: A light microscope is used with blue light of wavelength 450 nm and an objective of numerical aperture 1.30. Using d = 0.61 x wavelength / NA, calculate the smallest resolvable distance in nanometres.
questions.explanation: d = 0.61 x 450 / 1.30 = 211 nm. This is of the order of 200 nm, which is why structures smaller than this, such as ribosomes, cannot be resolved by light microscopy.

questions.stem: A pathologist counts 600 tumour nuclei in a Ki-67 immunostain and finds 168 positive. Calculate the Ki-67 labelling index as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The index is positive nuclei divided by total nuclei counted: 168 / 600 x 100 = 28%. Because Ki-67 marks cycling cells, a higher index indicates a more proliferative tumour.

questions.stem: Which statement about transmission electron microscopy of tissue is correct?

options.text: It uses ultrathin sections contrasted with heavy metals and can resolve ribosomes and membrane detail
It uses 5 micrometre sections and coloured dyes like H&E
It images only the surface of intact specimens
It resolves about 200 nm, the same as light microscopy

questions.correctOptionText: It uses ultrathin sections contrasted with heavy metals and can resolve ribosomes and membrane detail

distractorRationale.b: TEM needs sections of only 60-90 nm.
distractorRationale.d: TEM resolves about 1-2 nm in practice.

questions.explanation: TEM passes electrons through ultrathin, metal-contrasted sections to show ultrastructure. Its practical resolution in biological sections is about 1-2 nm, far better than light microscopy.

questions.stem: State the purpose of a PAS stain and of an immunohistochemical stain, and describe how each produces its signal.
markingGuide: PAS demonstrates carbohydrate-rich material such as glycogen, neutral mucin, basement membrane and fungal walls.
Periodic acid oxidises sugar diols to aldehydes that react with Schiff reagent to give magenta.
IHC identifies a specific antigen using an antibody.
A primary antibody binds the antigen; an enzyme-labelled secondary antibody converts a chromogen (e.g. DAB) to a coloured deposit.
Contrast chemical class staining with specific antibody binding.
questions.explanation: PAS is a chemical reaction for a molecular class, whereas IHC is a binding reaction for one antigen detected by an enzymatic colour change.

questions.stem: For each of the following targets choose a suitable stain and state the expected result: (a) fibrosis in liver, (b) reticulin framework, (c) acid-fast bacilli, (d) a specific cell-surface protein on tumour cells. Then explain one advantage of electron microscopy over light microscopy.
markingGuide: Fibrosis: Masson trichrome, collagen blue or green.
Specific protein: immunohistochemistry with a specific antibody and enzyme-labelled detection.
TEM resolves ultrastructure (about 1-2 nm in tissue) beyond the roughly 200 nm limit of light microscopy.
questions.explanation: Each target needs the matching stain, and TEM advantage is resolution of ultrastructure such as membranes and organelles.
